1280:
Authenticity is the quality of being real, genuine, and true — not fake, not copied, and not pretended. When something or someone has authenticity, it means they are exactly what they claim to be, nothing more and nothing less.

Think of it this way: if someone hands you a painting and says Picasso made it, that painting has authenticity only if Picasso actually painted it. If someone else copied it, even perfectly, the authenticity is gone. Authenticity is about the truth of something's actual origin or nature.

The most straightforward use of the word is about physical things. A signed letter, a historical document, a piece of ancient jewellery, a luxury product — all of these can be authentic or inauthentic. To call something authentic means it is the real, original thing and not a forgery, reproduction, or imitation.

A museum, for example, carefully verifies the authenticity of an artefact before displaying it — making sure it is genuinely old and genuinely what it claims to be. A certificate of authenticity attached to a piece of art is a document confirming it is the real thing.

This is where the word gets richer and more interesting, and where it is used most often in everyday life.

When we talk about a person's authenticity, we mean the quality of being true to who they really are — their real values, real feelings, and real beliefs — rather than playing a role or performing a version of themselves to please others.

A person with authenticity does not pretend to like things they don't like. They do not change their opinions based on who is in the room. They do not wear a social mask to seem more impressive or more likeable. Their inner world and their outer behaviour match. What you see is what you get.

Imagine two people who receive a compliment. The first person says "Thank you, that genuinely means a lot to me" — and they actually feel it. The second person says the exact same words, but they don't feel anything; they're just saying what they feel they're supposed to say. The first person is being authentic. The second is performing.

One crucial nuance: authenticity in a person does not mean being rude, blunt, or unfiltered. You can be warm, considerate, and tactful while being completely authentic. Authenticity is about honesty with yourself and acting from your real values — not an excuse for bad behaviour dressed up as "just being real."

We also use this word when talking about food, art, music, and cultural experiences. An "authentic Italian meal" is one prepared the way it genuinely would be in Italy — not a version modified and watered down for a different audience. Authentic jazz, authentic craftsmanship, an authentic folk festival — in each case, the word signals that the thing is the real deal, rooted in its true tradition or origin, not a shallow imitation of it.

One thing that makes personal authenticity difficult is that it first requires self-knowledge. You cannot be true to who you are if you don't understand who you are. This is why authenticity is often described as something people work toward over time — it involves honest self-reflection, the courage to accept your real values and feelings, and the willingness to live by them even when it's uncomfortable.

Social pressure constantly pulls people away from authenticity. We are often rewarded for telling people what they want to hear, for blending in, or for performing a version of ourselves that gets the most approval. Holding onto authenticity in the face of that pressure takes genuine self-awareness and effort.

Authenticity is the foundation of trust. When a person consistently shows up as their real self, others can trust them, because there is no gap between who they present themselves to be and who they actually are. Relationships built on authenticity tend to be deeper and more meaningful, because both people know they are engaging with something real.

In art, writing, and creative work, authentic expression — work that comes from a genuinely felt place — tends to resonate far more deeply with people than work that is manufactured or imitative. It carries a quality that is almost impossible to fake: it simply feels true.

It is not the same as being perfect. An authentic person makes mistakes — they just own them honestly rather than hiding them.

It is not the same as oversharing. Being authentic doesn't mean telling everyone everything about yourself. It means that what you do share is true and not performed.

It is not the same as being unchangeable. A person can grow, evolve, and genuinely change their mind over time and still be completely authentic — as long as those changes come from real internal growth, not from trying to impress someone.

It is not selfishness. Authenticity means acting from your true values, and for many people, those true values include deep care for others. Being genuinely kind is just as authentic as anything else.
Common Phrases to See It in Action

• "The museum verified the authenticity of the artefact." — Is it genuinely what it appears to be?
  • "I was moved by the authenticity of her performance." — She wasn't acting; she was genuinely feeling it.
  • "He struggles with authenticity in social situations." — He finds it hard to be his real self around others.
  • "The restaurant is celebrated for the authenticity of its recipes." — They use real, traditional methods, not shortcuts.
  • "She values authenticity over perfection." — She would rather be real than flawless.

Authenticity is the quality of being genuinely real and true — in objects, in people, and in experiences. For an object, it means being the real thing and not a forgery or copy. For a person, it means being honest and true to one's own values, feelings, and beliefs rather than pretending or performing. For a cultural experience or a piece of creative work, it means being rooted in its true tradition without distortion or dilution.

At its deepest level, authenticity is about alignment — the honest, uncorrupted match between what something truly is on the inside and how it presents itself to the world.
1281:
When we call something or someone authoritarian, we mean they demand strict, unquestioning obedience — and they use power, control, or force to get it, rather than earning people's willing cooperation.

Think of it this way: an authoritarian person or system says "You must obey because I said so" — not "Here's why this makes sense" or "Let's decide this together." The obedience is not optional. Discussion is not welcome. Disagreement is punished or silenced.

The adjective "authoritarian" is used to describe three main things:

1. Governments and political systems
An authoritarian government is one that concentrates all power in a single leader or a small group, denying ordinary citizens any meaningful say in how they are governed. Elections may not exist, or if they do, they are rigged. The press is controlled. People who criticize the government face punishment. Citizens are told what to think, what to say, and sometimes even what to believe. Examples of authoritarian regimes include single-party dictatorships or military-controlled governments where no one can legally challenge those in charge.

2. Leaders and people in positions of power
A person can be described as authoritarian when they rule over others by issuing commands and expecting complete compliance — whether that person is a political leader, a boss, a teacher, or even a parent. An authoritarian boss doesn't ask for your opinion on a decision; they simply tell you what to do and expect it done without question. An authoritarian parent makes all the rules at home and punishes any sign of pushback from their children, instead of explaining reasoning or allowing any independence.

3. Styles, structures, and systems
You can also describe a style of leadership, management, or parenting as authoritarian. It means the overall approach is built on strict control, rigid rules, blind obedience, and very little room for individual freedom or input.

To recognize something as authoritarian, look for these essential features:

Power concentrated at the top. One person or one group holds nearly all control. There are no meaningful checks — no systems to limit their power or hold them accountable.

Obedience is demanded, not earned. People are expected to comply simply because authority says so. The reasoning is rarely explained, and even if it is, questioning it is not tolerated.

Dissent is suppressed. Opposition, criticism, protest, or even mild disagreement is shut down — through punishment, intimidation, silencing, or force. The authoritarian system cannot tolerate being challenged.

Little to no individual freedom. People under an authoritarian system have very limited freedom to make their own choices — whether about their politics, speech, lifestyle, or beliefs — if those choices conflict with what the authority wants.

"Authoritarian" is almost always used with a negative connotation. When you call something authoritarian, you are implying that the control being exercised is excessive, unjust, oppressive, or disrespectful of human freedom and dignity. It carries the idea that people are being treated as subjects to be controlled rather than as individuals to be respected.

Even in softer, everyday contexts — like calling a manager or teacher "authoritarian" — it usually signals criticism. It suggests the person is too rigid, too controlling, and too dismissive of others' voices.

These two words look and sound similar, but they mean very different things — and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes learners make.

Authoritative means being a reliable, knowledgeable, and credible source of guidance. A doctor giving authoritative advice means their advice is trustworthy and well-informed. An authoritative book on a subject means it is the definitive, expert source. Being authoritative is generally positive.

Authoritarian means demanding obedience through power and control, not through knowledge or credibility. It is about dominance and enforcement, not expertise or trust.

A simple way to remember it: an authoritative person earns your trust through their knowledge. An authoritarian person demands your compliance through their power.

"Authoritarian" exists on a spectrum. At its most extreme, it describes brutal dictatorships that imprison or harm anyone who resists. In milder, everyday use, it might describe a teacher whose classroom is so rigidly controlled that students are afraid to ask questions, or a parent whose parenting style offers zero flexibility or explanation.

Regardless of degree, the word always points to the same essential quality: control that does not allow room for freedom, choice, or meaningful dissent.

• The country suffered for decades under an authoritarian regime that banned free speech and imprisoned political opponents.
  • Her authoritarian management style meant employees never felt comfortable sharing new ideas.
  • The new policies were criticized as authoritarian because they restricted what citizens could say online.
  • Growing up with an authoritarian father meant never being allowed to question a single household rule.
  • The school's authoritarian approach to discipline created fear rather than genuine respect.

It helps to know that "authoritarian" can also function as a noun (referring to a person: "He is an authoritarian"), and the related noun "authoritarianism" refers to the system, ideology, or practice of authoritarian rule as a whole.

If you ever need to recall it quickly: authoritarian describes any person, government, or system that demands strict obedience and exercises rigid control over others, leaving little to no room for freedom, individual choice, or meaningful challenge to authority.
1282:
Authoritarianism is a system of governing — or the belief in such a system — where one person or a small group holds power in an absolute or near-absolute way, with little or no genuine accountability to the people being governed. The people have no real, meaningful say in how they are ruled.

Think of it this way: in a healthy democracy, power flows upward from the people to their leaders. In authoritarianism, power flows downward from the ruler to the people — and the people must simply accept it.
What It Looks Like in Practice

An authoritarian system typically has several recognizable features, all of which tend to work together.

Concentrated power. Authority is held by one ruler, one party, one military, or one small elite group. There is no genuine sharing of power. Institutions that are supposed to act as checks — courts, parliaments, the press — either don't exist in a meaningful form, or they exist on paper but are controlled by the ruler in reality.

Suppression of opposition. Critics, rivals, journalists, protesters, and anyone who challenges the ruler's authority is silenced — through intimidation, imprisonment, exile, or worse. Free speech and free press are either heavily restricted or completely absent. Holding the "wrong" opinion can be dangerous.

No real accountability. In a democracy, a leader who abuses power can be voted out, taken to court, or removed from office. In an authoritarian system, the ruler is effectively above the law, or simply rewrites the law to protect themselves. Elections, if they happen at all, are rigged, staged, or meaningless.

Control of information. Authoritarian regimes frequently control what citizens are allowed to see, hear, and believe. State-run media promotes the ruler's version of reality, while independent journalism is banned or crushed. This keeps people misinformed, confused, or afraid to question the official story.

Rule through fear. Compliance is maintained not through the genuine trust or consent of the people, but through surveillance, threats, and punishment. Citizens learn to self-censor — to not say what they really think, even in private — because the consequences of dissent can be severe.
The Spectrum: It Is Not All-or-Nothing

Authoritarianism is not a single fixed state. It exists on a spectrum, from mild to extreme.

At the milder end, you might have a government that holds elections but manipulates them, restricts certain freedoms while allowing others, and punishes vocal critics but not ordinary citizens. Many countries today sit in this grey zone — outwardly resembling democracies, but hollowed out from within.

Further along the spectrum, you have full dictatorships: governments that ban political parties, control the economy entirely, imprison anyone who speaks out, and rule openly by force.

At the most extreme end sits totalitarianism — the most severe form of authoritarianism. A totalitarian regime doesn't just control the government; it seeks to control every aspect of life: what you read, what you watch, who you associate with, and even what you are supposed to think and believe. Nazi Germany under Hitler and the Soviet Union under Stalin are the defining historical examples.
How Authoritarian Regimes Come to Power

Authoritarianism doesn't always arrive suddenly. It can emerge through several paths.

Sometimes it comes through a military coup — the army simply seizes power by force, overthrows the existing government, and installs a general or junta as ruler.

Sometimes it comes through gradual erosion, often called "democratic backsliding." A leader is elected fairly and legitimately, but then, once in power, slowly dismantles the institutions designed to limit them — weakening courts, muzzling the press, changing laws to extend their own power, and eliminating rivals. This is a more subtle and increasingly common path, because it can look like legal and legitimate governance even as democracy quietly collapses.

It can also arise through revolution, inheritance (as in hereditary monarchies or family dynasties), or outright conquest.
How Authoritarian Regimes Stay in Power

Maintaining authoritarian control requires constant effort. Common tools include propaganda (shaping what people believe through controlled media and education), the cult of personality (presenting the leader as infallible, heroic, or even god-like, so that loyalty to the leader becomes almost a religion), secret police and mass surveillance (so people never know if they are being watched, and thus are afraid to act against the regime), and the systematic purging of rivals — removing anyone inside the system who might grow powerful enough to challenge the ruler. Rewarding those who are loyal with money, jobs, and protection, while punishing dissenters harshly, also keeps the inner circle in line.

Living under authoritarianism has profound consequences for everyday life. People lose freedom of speech — they cannot openly criticize the government. They lose freedom of the press — they cannot trust that news is accurate or independent. They lose freedom of assembly — gathering to protest or organize is dangerous or illegal. Political prisoners — people jailed not for crimes but for their beliefs, speech, or associations — are common. Corruption tends to flourish, because those in power can act without consequence. Human rights abuses — including torture, forced disappearance, and ethnic persecution — are well-documented features of authoritarian systems throughout history.

Beyond the obvious political dimension, there is a psychological toll: people become cautious, distrustful, and accustomed to self-censorship. The habit of hiding one's true thoughts can persist in a society even after an authoritarian regime ends.

While authoritarianism most commonly describes political systems, the word is also used more broadly in everyday life to describe any relationship or institution built on the same principles: absolute obedience demanded, no questioning tolerated, punishment for non-compliance.

An authoritarian parent is one who expects total obedience from their child, sets rigid rules without explanation, and punishes disobedience harshly — rather than reasoning with the child or allowing them any autonomy. An authoritarian boss runs a workplace where employees are expected to comply without question, feedback is unwelcome, and dissent is punished. The word can even describe schools, religious institutions, or clubs that operate on the same logic.
How It Relates to Similar Words

It helps to know how authoritarianism sits alongside related terms.

An autocracy is rule by a single person — it describes the structure. Authoritarianism describes the style and nature of rule (and can involve a small group, not just one person). A dictatorship typically refers to one person ruling with unchecked power, often obtained or held by force. Totalitarianism is the extreme end of authoritarianism, where the state seeks control over every corner of life. Fascism is a specific far-right authoritarian ideology that adds extreme nationalism, glorification of violence, and contempt for democracy and individual rights.

In short: all totalitarian systems are authoritarian, but not all authoritarian systems are totalitarian. And authoritarianism is the broader umbrella that covers all of these.

If you had to reduce it to its essence: authoritarianism is any system, style of rule, or belief that concentrates power in the hands of one person or a small group, demands obedience without accountability, and suppresses any challenge to that power.
1283:
At the heart of this word is one simple idea: being worthy of trust and belief — because of knowledge, skill, or confident power.

When something or someone is described as authoritative, it means they carry a kind of weight. People naturally listen to them, believe them, and follow them — not because they are forced to, but because they recognize that this person or source genuinely knows what they're talking about, or commands the situation with real confidence.

This word is used in two closely related but slightly different ways:

Sense 1 — Reliable, Expert, and Definitive (used for sources, statements, and information)

When a book, a study, a report, a statement, or a person's knowledge is called authoritative, it means it is the most trusted, most accurate, and most expert version available on that subject. It is the kind of source that settles the matter — you don't need to double-check it elsewhere.

Examples:

  • "This is the most authoritative book ever written on climate science."

Here, the book is written by leading experts, is deeply researched, and is fully trusted by the scientific community. It is the go-to source.

  • "The doctor gave an authoritative explanation of the disease."

Her explanation was so clear, expert, and well-grounded that it left no room for doubt.

  • "The report is considered the authoritative guide on child nutrition."

This means: if you want the most reliable, definitive information on child nutrition, this is the one report everyone points to.

Think of it this way: If 100 people were arguing about a topic and someone handed them an authoritative source, the argument would stop — because everyone trusts it.

Sense 2 — Commanding, Confident, and Respected (used for a person's manner, tone, or presence)

When we describe a person's behavior, voice, tone, or presence as authoritative, we mean they carry themselves with such confidence and clarity that people naturally pay attention and take them seriously. They don't beg to be heard — they just naturally are heard.

Examples:

  • "She spoke in an authoritative tone, and the room fell silent."

Her voice wasn't necessarily loud or aggressive — but it had a firmness and confidence that commanded attention.

  • "The coach had an authoritative presence on the field."

Players listened to him without question — not out of fear, but because he clearly knew what he was doing and projected it.

  • "He gave an authoritative nod, and the team moved forward."

Even a small gesture from him carried enough weight to guide others.

Think of it this way: An authoritative person walks into a room and people instinctively feel, "This person knows what they're doing. I should listen."
What Makes Something or Someone Authoritative?

There are a few ingredients that make something "authoritative":

  • Deep knowledge or expertise — you have genuinely mastered a subject.
  • A track record of being right or reliable — people have tested you and found you trustworthy.
  • Confidence without arrogance — you speak clearly and firmly, not nervously or boastfully.
  • Recognition by others — authoritativeness isn't just self-claimed. Others must acknowledge and accept it.

Note that last point carefully: you cannot simply declare yourself authoritative. It is something that others recognize in you based on what you know and how you carry yourself.
A Critical Distinction: Authoritative vs. Authoritarian

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word, because these two words look and sound similar but mean very different things.

AuthoritativeDeserving of trust and respect because of real knowledge or genuine confidence. A positive quality.
AuthoritarianDemanding strict obedience by force or dominance, without caring about others' input or rights. A negative quality.

Example:

  • A good teacher is authoritative — students listen because the teacher clearly knows the subject and commands respect.
  • A dictator is authoritarian — people obey not because they trust or respect him, but because they fear the consequences of not obeying.

An authoritative person leads with knowledge and earned confidence. An authoritarian person leads with control and force.

"Authoritative" is almost always a compliment. Calling a source, a person, or a statement authoritative signals high quality, deep reliability, and earned respect. It is the opposite of being vague, uncertain, untrustworthy, or amateur.

If someone calls your work authoritative, they are saying: "This is the real deal. This can be fully trusted."

Authoritative means: deserving to be fully trusted and listened to — either because of deep expertise and reliability (when describing information or sources), or because of confident, commanding, and credible presence (when describing a person's manner or tone).

It is a word that signals genuine quality and earned respect — not forced obedience, not self-proclaimed importance, but the kind of trust that others willingly and naturally give.
1284:
Authority means the recognized right to make decisions, give orders, or be trusted — and to have others accept that right and act accordingly.

The single most important word here is recognized. Authority is not just raw power (the ability to force something). It is legitimate power — power that other people see as valid, justified, and worth obeying. This distinction is what separates authority from, say, a threat or brute force.

1. The right to make decisions and have them obeyed

This is the most common meaning. A person or body in authority has a formal or socially accepted right to direct others, set rules, and take action — and others are expected to follow.

  • A judge has authority to sentence criminals — not because she is physically the strongest person in the courtroom, but because the legal system grants her that right.
  • A doctor has authority to prescribe medicine.
  • A manager has authority over the team she leads.
  • A government has authority to collect taxes from its citizens.

Two important things to notice here:

Authority is always bounded. A school principal has authority within the school, not on the street outside it. A local court's authority covers its own jurisdiction, not the whole country. This limit is sometimes called the scope or jurisdiction of someone's authority.

Authority can be delegated — passed downward. A CEO has authority, and she can give some of that authority to a department head, who can give some to a team leader. The right flows down the chain, but it originates from a recognized source at the top.

2. A person or body that holds official power

"Authority" — and especially its plural form "authorities" — often refers to the actual people or organizations that hold official power.

  • "The authorities investigated the crime." — meaning the police or government officials.
  • "You need to report this to the relevant authority." — meaning an official institution.
  • "The health authority issued new guidelines." — an official body responsible for public health.

In this sense, the word has essentially become a label for any official institution or official person with recognized power.

3. The right to be trusted and believed (expert authority)

This meaning has nothing to do with commanding people. Here, "authority" refers to a person whose deep knowledge or expertise earns them the right to be believed and relied upon.

  • "She is an authority on medieval history."
  • "He is a leading authority in cancer research."
  • "This book is considered the authority on the subject."

When you call someone an authority on a topic, you mean: if they say something about that topic, you should trust it, because they have thought about it and studied it more deeply than almost anyone else.

This kind of authority is earned through knowledge, not granted by appointment. You become an authority by accumulating deep, proven expertise over time. It cannot simply be declared — others must recognize it.
Authority vs. Power — The Most Important Distinction

Power is the ability to make things happen or control others. Authority is the right to do so, as recognized by others.

  • A bully has power over a weaker person but has no authority — nobody sees his dominance as legitimate.
  • A referee at a football match has authority — players follow his calls not because he is stronger than them, but because everyone has agreed that he has the right to make those decisions within the game.

This is why authority is fragile in a way that raw power is not. Authority depends on other people continuing to accept it as legitimate. The moment a population stops recognizing a government as rightful, its authority collapses — even if its armies still stand. A manager who loses the trust and respect of her team loses her authority in practice, even if she still holds the job title.

Authority has different sources depending on the context:

  • Law and formal rules — A judge's authority comes from the legal system.
  • Organizational structure — A manager's authority comes from the company's hierarchy.
  • Expertise and knowledge — A scientist's authority over her field comes from years of research and proven accuracy.
  • Tradition and social norms — A parent's authority over a young child is recognized across nearly all human cultures.
  • Consent — An elected leader's authority comes from people choosing them. This is widely considered the most legitimate source in modern societies.

There is one more important form worth knowing: moral authority. This is the standing to guide, judge, or persuade others based not on a formal position or expertise, but on perceived moral integrity or virtue.

  • A person who has lived honestly, sacrificed for others, and acted with consistent fairness earns moral authority — people listen to them on ethical matters because of who they are, not what role they hold.
  • Conversely, a politician caught in corruption is said to have lost moral authority, meaning others no longer feel that person has any right to tell them how to live or act.

Moral authority cannot be assigned or inherited. It is entirely earned through behavior and character.

"In authority" — Holding a position of recognized power.
"Always report safety concerns to someone in authority."

"On good authority" — From a trustworthy, reliable source.
"I have it on good authority that the project is cancelled" — meaning a knowledgeable or credible person told you, so you believe it.

"With authority" — In a confident, commanding way that signals expertise or power.
"She answered every question with authority."

"Under the authority of" — Subject to someone's jurisdiction or control.
"The office operates under the authority of the regional government."

"Acting on someone's authority" — Doing something because another person authorized you to do it, so the right ultimately comes from them.
"She signed the contract acting on the director's authority."

Think of authority as power with a social contract attached. When someone has authority, it means:

  1. They have a right — to decide, to act, or to be believed.
  2. Others recognize and accept that right.
  3. That acceptance is what makes the authority real and functional.

Strip away the recognition, and authority disappears — no matter how much formal power the person technically holds. This is what makes authority both one of the most important organizing forces in human society, and one of the most fragile.
1285:
To authorize something means to officially give permission for it to happen — or to officially give someone the right to do something.

The key word is officially. This isn't casual permission like a friend saying "sure, go ahead." It's a formal act where someone with real power and authority grants a right, access, or ability to someone who didn't have it before (or couldn't act without that approval).

When someone authorizes something, three things are always present:

  1. A person or body with power — the one doing the authorizing. They must actually have the authority themselves. A random employee can't authorize company spending; a judge can't authorize something outside their legal power.
  2. A recipient — either a person, a group, a machine/system, or even an action itself, who or which is being authorized.
  3. A specific right or action — authorization is almost never open-ended. It applies to something specific: a payment, an entry, a decision, an action.
What Exactly Happens When You Authorize Something?

Before authorization: the person/system cannot (or should not) act.
After authorization: they can and may act — legitimately, without consequence.

Authorization is like flipping a switch. It changes the status of an action from "not permitted" to "officially permitted."

And importantly, it creates accountability. The authorized person can now act, but the authorizer also takes on some responsibility for having granted that right.
The Many Contexts Where It's Used

This word appears everywhere because permission-granting is a universal concept:

In organizations and business:
"The CEO authorized the $5 million investment."
"She was authorized to sign contracts on behalf of the company."
— Here, someone in charge formally hands decision-making power to another.

In banking and finance:
"The bank authorized the payment."
"Your card was not authorized."
— The bank checks whether the transaction is legitimate and either unlocks it or blocks it.

In law and government:
"Congress authorized the use of military force."
"The court authorized a search of the premises."
— A governing body officially permits an action that has legal weight.

In technology and computers:
"The app was authorized to access your contacts."
"You need to authorize this device before logging in."
— A system or user grants a program or person the right to access data or functionality.

In everyday formal settings:
"Only authorized personnel may enter."
"I am not authorized to discuss that."
— "Authorized" here marks who has been officially cleared versus who hasn't.
What Makes Authorization Different from Just Allowing Something?

This is worth understanding carefully, because several words are close in meaning but not identical.

Allow is informal and passive. If you allow someone to borrow your pen, you're just not stopping them. There's no formal power involved, no transfer of rights, no record.

Authorize is formal and active. It creates a right. It implies a system — rules, hierarchy, accountability.

You allow your friend to borrow your umbrella.
You authorize an employee to access the company's confidential files.

Permit sits somewhere in between. It can be formal (a government issues building permits), but informally it's used like "allow." Authorize is almost always on the formal end.

Approve means you agree something is good or acceptable — it's about your opinion or endorsement. Authorize means you grant the right to act — it's about power and permission. These are related but different:

  • A manager might approve of a team member's idea but not yet authorize spending money on it.
  • A bank officer might personally dislike a transaction but still authorize it because it meets all the rules.

Empower is about giving someone capability, strength, or confidence — often used in motivational or social contexts. Authorize is specifically about official, formal permission.
The Passive Form — Very Common and Important

You'll often see "authorize" in the passive voice:

  • "You are authorized to proceed."
  • "This system is not authorized."
  • "She was not authorized to make that decision."

Here, the subject is receiving the authorization rather than giving it. The passive form emphasizes the status of the person or thing — whether they hold that official right or not.

Authorization is not necessarily permanent. What is authorized can be de-authorized or unauthorized — meaning the right is taken back. Access cards get deactivated. Approvals get reversed. Permissions get removed. This makes authorization dynamic: it's a status that can change.
A Subtle but Important Point: Authorization Implies Legitimacy

When an action is authorized, it becomes legitimate within whatever system governs it. It's not just that you can do it — it means doing it is proper, sanctioned, and defensible. If something goes wrong, an authorized person can say "I was permitted to do this." Without authorization, the same action could be seen as overstepping, illegal, or improper — even if it turned out to be harmless.

This is why the word carries weight. It's not just about unlocking a door; it's about the formal, official, recognized right to walk through it.

To authorize is to formally grant someone (or something) the official right or permission to do something, by a person or body that has the power to make that grant — transforming an action from "not permitted" into "legitimately permitted."
1286:
Authorship means the fact or condition of being the creator of something — most commonly a written work like a book, article, poem, or script, but sometimes also a theory, idea, or plan.

Think of it this way: when someone writes a novel, two things become true at once. First, a book now exists in the world. Second, someone is responsible for bringing it into existence. That second part — the relationship between the creator and the thing they created — is what authorship captures.
Breaking It Down Into Its Two Main Senses

The word carries two closely related but slightly different meanings, and understanding both is key.

Sense 1: The Identity of Who Created Something

This is the most common use. When people ask "Who wrote this?" or "Where did this come from?", they are asking about authorship.

"The authorship of the anonymous letter was never confirmed."
"There is a long debate about the authorship of Shakespeare's plays."

Here, authorship simply means: who is the author? It refers to the origin of a work — the specific person (or group) it came from.

Sense 2: The Profession or Activity of Writing

Authorship can also refer to the occupation, practice, or experience of being a writer — writing as a craft or career.

"She found great satisfaction in authorship."
"Authorship demands patience, discipline, and a love of language."

In this sense, it does not point to a specific work. Instead, it describes what authors do and what that life or activity involves.

Understanding the word fully means understanding what it quietly assumes:

1. Originality
Authorship implies that the work came from your own mind. If you copy someone else's work word for word and call it yours, you do not have genuine authorship — that would be plagiarism. Authorship carries the idea of original creation.

2. Responsibility
To claim authorship of something is to say: "I made this. I stand behind it." It is both a claim of credit and an acceptance of accountability. If a scientist publishes a research paper, their authorship means they are responsible for what it says.

3. Ownership (in a practical sense)
Authorship is closely tied to the idea that the creator has a special relationship with their work — a kind of intellectual ownership. This is why legal systems recognise copyright, which protects authors' rights over their creations. Authorship is the foundation on which those rights rest.

The word appears in many real-world contexts. Here are the most important ones:

Sole authorship — One person created the work entirely on their own.

"The novel was entirely her own work — sole authorship was never in question."

Co-authorship / Joint authorship — Two or more people created something together. Each person shares authorship.

"The research paper lists three names because it was a work of joint authorship."

Disputed authorship — There is disagreement or uncertainty about who actually created something.

"The disputed authorship of those ancient texts has fascinated historians for centuries."

Anonymous authorship — A work exists, but the identity of its creator is unknown or deliberately hidden.

"The book was published under a pen name, keeping its authorship a mystery."

Ghost authorship — Someone creates a work, but another person's name is put on it (common in celebrity memoirs, for example). The real authorship is hidden.

Corporate or institutional authorship — Sometimes an organisation, rather than an individual, is listed as the author of a document or report.
How Authorship Differs From Similar Words

It helps to place "authorship" alongside words that seem similar but mean something slightly different:

  • Writing — the act of putting words on paper. You can write something without being its true author (e.g., a typist who transcribes someone else's dictation).
  • Creatorship / Creation — broader terms that apply to any kind of creative act (art, music, invention). Authorship is more specifically tied to written or intellectual works.
  • Ownership — you can own something you didn't create (e.g., you can buy a painting). Authorship is about who made it, not necessarily who currently holds it.
  • Credit — you can receive credit for something as a team member without being its author. Authorship is a more specific and stronger claim.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Authorship = the "who made it and what that means" of a creative work.

Whenever you see or use this word, it is doing one of two jobs: either pointing to the person behind a work, or describing the life and craft of being a writer. Both uses circle around the same central truth — that every piece of writing, every idea put into words, traces back to a human mind that brought it into being.

Autism (also called Autism Spectrum Disorder, or ASD) is a condition that affects how a person's brain develops and works. It is not an illness, a disease, or something that happens to a person later in life — a person is born with it, and it stays with them for their entire life.

The simplest way to understand it: the brain of an autistic person is wired differently from the brain of a non-autistic person. This different wiring changes how they perceive the world, how they communicate, how they connect with others, and how they process their senses (like sound, light, and touch). It affects almost every aspect of how a person experiences life.
The Word "Spectrum" — and Why It Matters

Autism is called a spectrum condition. A spectrum means a wide range. Think of a rainbow — it has many colours, each different from the next, but they are all part of the same rainbow.

Similarly, autism looks very different from one person to another. One autistic person might speak fluently, hold a job, and live independently, while another might not speak at all and need support with daily tasks. One might struggle intensely in social situations, while another might be highly social but process conversations in a different way. One might have very high academic intelligence, and another might have intellectual disabilities alongside their autism.

Because of this enormous variety, there is a saying in the autism community: "If you've met one autistic person, you've met one autistic person." No two are exactly alike.

This is why professionals stopped using terms like "mild" or "severe" autism and instead describe how much support a person needs in daily life — ranging from needing a little support to needing very substantial support.
The Three Core Areas Autism Affects

Autism consistently affects three main areas of a person's experience:

1. Social Communication

Autistic people often communicate differently. This does not mean they have nothing to say — it means the way they send and receive messages works differently.

For example, they may:

  • Struggle to read unspoken social rules (like when to take turns in conversation, or what a facial expression means)
  • Take language very literally (if you say "it's raining cats and dogs," they may be confused because no animals are falling from the sky)
  • Prefer direct, clear, honest communication over hints and small talk
  • Have difficulty understanding sarcasm or jokes that rely on tone
  • Communicate more comfortably in writing than in speech

Importantly, many autistic people deeply want to connect with others — the challenge is not the desire, but the way communication works for them.

2. Repetitive Behaviours and Restricted Interests

Autistic people often have patterns, routines, and interests that are deeply important to them.

This may look like:

  • Following very specific daily routines, and feeling significant distress if those routines are broken
  • Moving their body in repetitive ways — rocking, hand-flapping, spinning — called stimming (short for self-stimulatory behaviour). Stimming helps autistic people regulate their emotions and manage sensory experiences
  • Developing an extremely deep, passionate, detailed interest in one or a few specific topics — sometimes called a "special interest." An autistic child might know every fact about trains, planets, or a particular video game, with a level of depth that goes far beyond what most people would find typical

These patterns are not random quirks. They serve important functions: they provide predictability, comfort, and control in a world that can often feel overwhelming.

3. Sensory Processing Differences

This is one of the most significant and often overlooked aspects of autism. Autistic people frequently experience the world through their senses very differently.

Some are hypersensitive (over-sensitive), meaning:

  • A sound that most people barely notice — a distant hum, a crowd, a fluorescent light — can feel unbearably loud and painful
  • Certain clothing textures can feel physically intolerable
  • Bright lights can feel blinding
  • Certain smells or food textures can cause intense discomfort or make eating very difficult

Some are hyposensitive (under-sensitive), meaning:

  • They may not notice pain as easily
  • They may seek out intense sensory experiences, like pressing tightly against things or spinning

Many autistic people are a mix of both — hypersensitive in some areas, hyposensitive in others.

Autism is present from birth. However, signs are typically noticeable in early childhood — often by ages 2 to 3. A child might not point at things to share interest, may not respond to their name, may develop language and then stop using it, or may show repetitive behaviours.

That said, some people — especially those who are very intelligent or who have learned to mask (hide or suppress their autistic traits to fit in socially) — may not receive a diagnosis until later in life, sometimes even in adulthood. Many women and girls in particular are diagnosed later because they tend to be better at masking from a young age.

A formal diagnosis is given by qualified professionals — typically psychologists or psychiatrists — who assess the person's behaviour, development, and experiences through interviews, observation, and questionnaires.

The exact cause of autism is not fully understood, but science has established some clear things:

  • Genetics play a very large role. Autism runs in families, and many specific genes have been linked to it. If one identical twin has autism, the other has a very high chance of also having it
  • Brain development in the womb is involved — the differences in an autistic brain begin before birth
  • It is influenced by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, though no single cause has been identified

What does not cause autism:

  • Vaccines — this has been studied extensively and the claim is completely false. The original study that suggested this was fraudulent and has been fully discredited
  • Bad parenting
  • Childhood trauma (though trauma can worsen some difficulties)
  • Too much screen time

Because there are many misconceptions, it helps to be clear:

  • Autism is not an intellectual disability. Intellectual ability in autistic people spans the full range — from profound intellectual disability to extremely high intelligence. Many autistic people have average or above-average intelligence
  • Autism is not the same as being introverted or shy. Shyness is about feeling nervous around people. Autism is about how the brain processes the whole world
  • Autism is not caused by being "cold" or emotionally distant. Autistic people absolutely feel emotions — often very deeply. They may express or process emotions differently, but they are not unfeeling
  • Autism is not something that can be "cured." It is not a broken state that needs fixing. It is a different neurological profile

Because autism involves a differently wired brain, it also often comes with genuine strengths:

  • Attention to detail — noticing things others miss
  • Deep focus — the ability to concentrate intensely on areas of interest
  • Pattern recognition — seeing connections and systems that others overlook
  • Honesty and directness — many autistic people are exceptionally genuine and straightforward
  • Memory — particularly strong memory for facts within areas of interest
  • Loyalty — many autistic people are deeply committed and reliable in their relationships

Many autistic people have made extraordinary contributions in science, mathematics, art, music, and technology. Some researchers believe that figures like Alan Turing (the father of modern computing) may have been autistic, though historical diagnosis is always uncertain.

A growing movement in psychology and society is neurodiversity — the idea that differences in how brains work are a natural and valuable part of human variation, not defects to be eliminated.

From this perspective, autism is not simply a disorder but a different cognitive style — one that brings both challenges and strengths, and that deserves understanding, accommodation, and respect rather than just treatment aimed at making autistic people appear more "normal."

This does not mean ignoring the very real difficulties autism can cause. It means understanding that the goal should be supporting autistic people in living well on their own terms, not erasing who they are.

If you had to summarise the entire word in a single sentence:

Autism is a lifelong, inborn condition in which the brain develops differently, affecting how a person communicates, connects socially, processes sensory information, and engages with the world — showing up uniquely in every individual and bringing both challenges and distinctive strengths.

An autobiography is a book — or a long written account — in which a person tells the story of their own life, written by themselves, in their own words.

Think of it this way: You sit down and write a book about your life, from your childhood memories, your struggles and victories, your relationships, your career — all the way to where you are today. That book is your autobiography.
The Three Golden Rules of an Autobiography

For something to qualify as an autobiography, three things must be true at the same time:

  1. The subject is the author. The person writing the book and the person the book is about are the exact same individual. You are writing about yourself.
  2. It covers life as a whole. An autobiography isn't about just one event or one chapter of life. It surveys a person's entire life — or at least a very large and meaningful stretch of it — usually in the order things actually happened (chronologically).
  3. It is non-fiction. Everything in it is presented as real and true. It is not a made-up story. It is a factual, personal account of real events, real people, and real experiences.

Because you are the one writing about yourself, an autobiography is almost always written in the first person — using words like I, me, my, and we. For example:

"I was born in a small village. My mother was a schoolteacher, and my father worked long hours at the factory..."

This first-person voice is what gives autobiographies their intimate, personal, and direct feeling — as if the author is sitting across from you and simply talking to you about their life.

A well-written autobiography usually walks you through:

  • Childhood and early life — where the person grew up, what their family was like, and early memories that shaped them.
  • Formative experiences — turning points, hardships, discoveries, and relationships that changed who they are.
  • Achievements and failures — the highs and lows of their career, creative work, or public life.
  • Personal growth — how they changed, what they learned, and who they became over time.
  • Reflections — their thoughts and feelings about their own life, looking back from the present moment.
How It Is Different from Similar Things

This is where many learners get confused, so let's clear this up completely.

Autobiography vs. Biography
A biography is also a book about a person's life — but it is written by someone else. If a journalist writes a detailed book about Elon Musk's life, that is a biography. If Elon Musk writes about his own life himself, that is an autobiography. The single biggest difference is simply: who holds the pen.

Autobiography vs. Memoir
A memoir is very close to an autobiography — it is also a person writing about their own life — but there is a subtle and important difference. An autobiography aims to cover the whole sweep of a life, generally from beginning to present. A memoir, on the other hand, zooms in on a specific period, theme, or set of experiences. For example, a person might write a memoir only about their years in prison, or only about their battle with illness, or only about growing up poor. An autobiography is broader and more complete; a memoir is narrower and more focused. All memoirs are a kind of autobiographical writing, but not all autobiographies are memoirs.

Autobiography vs. Diary or Journal
A diary or journal is a private, day-to-day personal record — notes you write for yourself, not for a reading audience. An autobiography is consciously shaped, edited, and written for readers. It is a literary work meant to be published and shared with the world.

Sometimes a famous person will tell their life story out loud — in long recorded interviews or conversations — and a professional writer (called a ghostwriter) will then shape and write those stories into a proper book. Even in this case, the book is still called an autobiography, because the life, voice, memories, and perspective belong entirely to the person whose name is on the cover. The ghostwriter is simply a craftsperson helping put the words on paper.

• Long Walk to Freedom by Nelson Mandela — Mandela wrote about his childhood in rural South Africa, his activism against apartheid, his 27 years in prison, and his path to becoming South Africa's first democratic president.
  • The Story of My Experiments with Truth by Mahatma Gandhi — Gandhi wrote about his personal, spiritual, and political journey in his own words.
  • The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank — while technically a diary, it is widely considered one of history's most powerful pieces of autobiographical writing, as Anne recorded her own real experiences hiding during the Holocaust.
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

• She spent three years writing her autobiography before finally publishing it.
  • His autobiography revealed details about his childhood that the public had never known.
  • The autobiography of the legendary musician became a bestseller overnight.
  • Reading someone's autobiography is one of the most personal ways to understand their life.

An autobiography is an act of self-documentation and self-expression. It is a person saying: "Here is my life. Here is what I lived through, what I felt, what I learned, and who I am." It gives readers a direct, intimate window into another human being's entire existence — told with the unique authority that only the person who actually lived that life can have.

An autocracy is a system of government in which one single person holds complete and unlimited power over an entire country. That one person — called an autocrat — makes all the important decisions alone, without needing anyone's approval, and nobody has the legal or political authority to stop them, overrule them, or hold them accountable.

Think of it this way: in most modern governments, power is shared and controlled. Laws limit what leaders can do. Courts can say "no, that's illegal." Citizens can vote leaders out. In an autocracy, none of that applies to the ruler. They are, essentially, above everything and everyone.
What Makes a Government an Autocracy?

There are three defining features that, together, make a government an autocracy:

1. Power concentrated in one person.
All major decisions — about war, law, economy, and citizens' lives — flow from a single individual. There is no meaningful co-ruler, no cabinet that can override them, and no legislative body with real authority.

2. No accountability.
The ruler does not answer to the people, to a constitution, or to any institution. They cannot be legally removed from power through elections, impeachment, or votes of no confidence. If accountability exists at all, it exists only on paper, not in practice.

3. No effective checks and balances.
In healthy governments, different branches (executive, legislative, judicial) watch over each other to prevent any one branch from becoming too powerful. In an autocracy, those checks either don't exist or have been made meaningless. Courts, parliaments, and laws serve the ruler, not the other way around.
How Does an Autocrat Stay in Power?

An autocracy doesn't simply declare itself and then run smoothly. Autocrats use a combination of tools to maintain their grip:

  • Force and fear — Police, the military, and intelligence agencies are used to suppress opposition. People who speak out risk imprisonment, violence, or worse.
  • Propaganda — State-controlled media shapes what citizens hear, read, and believe, often portraying the ruler as heroic, necessary, or divinely chosen.
  • Elimination of rivals — Political opponents, independent journalists, and powerful institutions are weakened, co-opted, or destroyed.
  • Loyalty networks — The ruler rewards loyal supporters (military generals, business elites, party members) with wealth and privilege, giving them a personal reason to keep the autocrat in power.

Autocracy is a broad category. It contains several specific forms:

  • Absolute monarchy — The ruler is a king or queen (or emperor) who inherited their position and faces no legal limits on their power. The historical Tsars of Russia and many ancient pharaohs of Egypt are examples.
  • Dictatorship — The ruler typically came to power through force (a military coup, for example) rather than inheritance. Adolf Hitler's Germany and Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union are defining examples.
  • One-party state — Technically, a party is in charge, but in practice, the top individual within that party holds all real power. North Korea under the Kim family is a modern example.

What all of these share is the same root: one person, unchecked power.
Autocracy vs. Similar Words (and How They Differ)

These words are closely related to autocracy but are not identical:

  • Democracy — The direct opposite. Power belongs to the people, exercised through free elections, free speech, and independent courts.
  • Oligarchy — Rule by a small group of people (wealthy elites, a military council, etc.), not just one person. An oligarchy is not an autocracy unless one person within the group eventually dominates everyone else.
  • Totalitarianism — A more extreme form of autocracy. Not only does the ruler control the government, but they attempt to control all aspects of life — culture, religion, family, thought, and expression. All totalitarian states are autocracies, but not all autocracies are fully totalitarian.
  • Authoritarianism — A broader term for any system where political freedom is severely restricted and the ruler governs without meaningful consent. Autocracy is a specific, extreme kind of authoritarianism — the kind where one individual holds all the power.
  • Tyranny — Historically, this referred to a ruler who seized power illegitimately and governed cruelly. Today, it's often used interchangeably with autocracy but carries a stronger moral judgment — it emphasizes the abuse of power, not just the structure of it.
How the Word Is Used in Practice

In its strictest sense, "autocracy" is a political science term used to describe a form of government. For example:

"Russia under the Tsars was a classic autocracy — the emperor's word was law, and no institution could legally challenge him."

"The country descended into autocracy after the military coup dissolved the parliament and suspended the constitution."

However, you will also encounter the word used more loosely in everyday language to describe any person — not just a national leader — who exercises excessive, unchecked control over others:

"He ran the company like an autocracy — every decision went through him, and no one else's opinion mattered."

This looser use is common and understood, but when used in political or academic writing, autocracy specifically refers to governmental systems.

Knowing the word family helps you recognize this concept in different forms:

  • Autocracy (noun) — the system itself ("living under an autocracy")
  • Autocrat (noun) — the person who rules ("the autocrat signed the decree")
  • Autocratic (adjective) — describing the style of rule ("an autocratic leader," "autocratic tendencies")
  • Autocratically (adverb) — describing how something is done ("the country was governed autocratically")
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: an autocracy is a government where one person rules with total, unchecked power, answerable to no one.
